subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, March 9, consideration of the motion of Hon. Charles A. Dunning (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before moving the
adjournment of the debate last night I attempted to show that we have approximately
200,000	square miles of fishing ground available to the fishermen of the maritime provinces; in other words, that we have nearly three times as large an area in fishing grounds as we have under cultivation.
I wish briefly to review the early history of our fisheries, in so far as they have reference to the maritime provinces. We find that since
the discovery of America, fisheries have been a matter of vital importance in Canadian development. The first grant in connection with fisheries was made by the King of France to De Monts in the year 1603. Fishing, therefore, may well be regarded as one of the first industries prosecuted by Europeans in what is to-day the Dominion of Canada, and it has never ceased to yield a yearly harvest.
It is estimated that in the year 1550, or thereabouts, the combined fleets of all countries in the north Atlantic numbered about 1,500 vessels. The position of land adjoining the fishing banks was important only in so far as it provided a means of drying or curing fish products caught adjoining the said land. We go first to the island of Cape Breton and find the early village of Cheticamp. The territory was at that time under the control of the French. Next we come to the mainland of Nova Scotia, and note that at Liverpool in 1760 they had 16 fishing vessels. Port La Tour and the Pubnicos were important early fishing settlements. In 1713, for example, at Canso, with a population of about 1,000 persons, there were 100,000 quintals of fish caught. Proceeding to New Brunswick we find that in 1765 William Davidson established a salmon fishery on the Miramichi river. There were other fishing settlements at Grand Anse, Campo Bello, and Deer Islands. In Prince Edward Island they, too, had settlements connected with the early fishing industry.
I refer to that part of our history to-day because we in the maritime provinces hope there may be something in store for us in the future, because our industries are so well established and of such long duration.
The fisheries of the maritime provinces can be divided into three parts. We have what we know as the deep fisheries, the inshore fisheries and the inland fisheries. In my observations to-day I am going to deal with the production of what we describe as ground fish, caught by the first two methods-deep sea fishing and inshore fishing.
The principal kinds of ground fish caught are cod, haddock, halibut, and hake. The prosperity or depression of the fishermen has up to the present depended upon the extent of his catch of these types of fish. I am not unmindful of the fact that the lobster industry has in some districts developed into their principal industry. However, it is carried on only in certain seasons, and is limited as to quantity of production.
Other types of fishing-fishing for mackerel, sardines, salmon, smelts, alewives, sword fish, tuna, shell fish, scallops, oysters and clams are either carried on only during certain seasons or in certain areas. Taking the mari-
The Budget-Mr. Pottier

time province fisheries as a whole I am of opinion that they can be considered only as a complement of the main industry as above indicated. I do not wish to be understood as saying they are not important, because they mean a great deal to some districts, and in those districts their development must be attended to.
The remainder of my remarks will therefore be directed to a discussion of the general situation, in so far as the development of the ground fish, so-called, can be carried on. That is the direction in which parliament should apply itself particularly. I have before me indications of what has taken place in Canada in past five-year periods, in relation to cod. These figures, relating to catches and values of cod, are a fair indication of what has happened in connection with other species:

It is of interest to note that in the production of such fish the. maritime provinces have not held their own with world production. I find that the production of cod in those countries which produce this type of fish is on the increase. In 1919 the fishermen of Norway caught 359,004,000 pounds. In 1927 the catch had increased to 808,649,000 pounds. In 1932 the catch totalled 661,746,000 pounds. In the Faroe islands they caught
99.888.000	pounds in 1919, and 148,968,000 pounds in 1932. In Iceland they caught
168.885.000	pounds in 1919 and 457,778,000 pounds in 1932. I could go on to show how other countries with which we have to compete have been increasing their production, while ours has been going down. The figures I give are the best available.
In my opinion these figures indicate three things. First, that Canada has gone back; second, that we have not held our own in world production; and third, that we have not kept step with European countries. This unhappy and unfortunate situation must come to an end. These figures tell the story of the maritime fisherman; they explain why we find him bankrupt and why the industry in some areas has taken on the appearance of failure.
The status of a large number of fishermen in the maritimes has become desperate. For

example, in one district in my riding, which was once a prosperous and successful fishing district, the catch for 1935 followed this general trend. I want to see it improved. I should like to give some examples of the earnings of some of the fishing boats. I shall not give names, referring to them only by number. Boat number one, with a crew of 22 men, fished for fourteen weeks. It stocked $4,000, and the average share per man per week was $4. Boat number two, with a crew of 21 men, fished nine weeks. It stocked $2,272, and the average share per man per week was about $2. Boat number three, with a crew of 18 men, fished twenty-two weeks. It stocked $3,600, and the average share per man per week was about $1. Boat number four with a crew of 12 men, fished 13 weeks. It stocked $2,100 and the average share per man per week was $5.50. Boat number five, with a crew of six men, fished 13 weeks, and the average share per man per week was fifty cents.
As a further example of the public feeling in connection with this industry, I quote from the Halifax Herald:
The shore fishing industry in Nova Scotia is down to hard rocks of want. They are crushed by an industry out of control, a juggernaut headed toward doom. They need help and it must be forthcoming.
The special investigations carried on by this Nova Scotia newspaper show the seriousness of the situation. In the end the reports published should help a great deal to bring about a new standard in the industry.
I could go on and give a word picture of the conditions existing in a number of districts where the fishermen have been the unfortunate victims of the vicious circle I have mentioned above. These districts were successful and prosperous at confederation, but now the families living therein are undernourished, the children hungry, and they are forced to live with little hope for the future in houses with leaky roofs on rocky points of land. I do not want to exaggerate and have the house think that this is a picture of every district in the maritimes. Some districts have been more fortunate than others, particularly those where a fresh fish trade has been developed. I felt obliged to give this picture because I am convinced that these conditions are not generally known, and that is one of the reasons why they are allowed to continue to exist. I have in mind one particular case where two fishermen were drowned during a storm. This was one instance where human effort and endurance were unable to withstand the elements, the hardships and hazards of the industry.

The Budget-Mr. Pettier
I am convinced that the fisheries of the maritime provinces have been neglected, particularly when I look around and see what other countries producing the same type of fish are doing. I should like to refer to the assistance given by other countries with which we compete. This assistance can be divided into three categories, direct assistance, indirect assistance and emergency relief. I find that direct assistance in connection with fishing operations is given by Germany and Japan. Assistance in connection with exports is given by Denmark, France, the Irish Free State, Italy, Newfoundland and Norway. Assistance in the construction of vessels is given by Germany, Japan and Newfoundland. Assistance in the repair of vessels is given by Germany and Japan. Assistance through the establishment of freezing plants is given by Japan and Norway. Other direct assistance is given by Italy, Japan and Newfoundland.
Indirect assistance by way of government loans and guarantees is given by Denmark, France, Germany, Iceland, the Irish Free State, Italy, The Netherlands, Newfoundland, Norway, Portugal, the United Kingdom and the United States. Assistance by way of home market promotion is given by Denmark, France, Germany and Japan. Assistance by way of preferential transportation rates is given by Germany and Newfoundland. Tax or duty exemption is given by Italy, Japan, Mexico, Newfoundland, the United Kingdom and the United States. Other indirect assistance is given by Italy, Japan, Mexico, Newfoundland and Norway. Emergency relief is provided by Germany, Great Britain and the United States.
Let us see what Canada has done. We have the Fisherman's Loan Act which was passed in 1935, but I understand that up to the present time no loans have been made under this act. This country gives no assistance in connection with exports or in connection with the construction of vessels. We give no assistance in the repair of vessels nor have we any provision for emergency relief. I am not forgetting .the item voted for the development of deep sea fisheries, as well as the vote of S500,000 last year for general relief. Under that vote all that a fisherman in my constituency could get was a loan of S20 added to a similar amount given by the province of Nova Scotia. Even that small amount was the first he has been able to borrow in connection with his industry. I make no reference to the $160,000 granted under the Halifax award as I consider that to represent simply the interest on money that belongs to us. I cannot treat it as being assistance given by this government.
I should like to mention some other features which have had an effect upon the fishermen in the maritime provinces. We lost the best market we ever had when the Fordney-Mc-Cumber tariff was put into effect in the United States. Russia and Germany, which countries were formerly importers of fish, taking the surplus products of Holland, Great Britain, Norway and France, have now built up fishing fleets and have forced these other countries to find other markets. These countries have entered the West Indies and South American markets, as well as the markets of Spain and Portugal, displacing Canada. This has been possible through force of circumstances and by means of the assistance provided by their governments The immigration laws of the United States prevent our fishermen from signing on American fishing vessels, as was the custom in former years. This has meant that an increased number of fishermen have had to remain in Canada. Then the beam trawler has thrown a large number of fishermen out of employment, as by this method of fishing a smaller number of men are employed to catch the same amount of fish.
As a result of these and other causes what do we find regarding the export of these products	to other	countries? I	will refer

I submit that those figures go to show why the fisherman of the maritime provinces finds himself in the position in which he is. They relate to only a few of the importing countries, but they indicate the general trend.
Up to the present time the federal, policy under all governments has been one of regulation and control; in other words, a policy of restrictions and reservations. This has come about, presumably, because of the interpretation placed upon the words "sea coast and inland fisheries," as under the British North America Act those subjects were passed on to the federal government, and the result to the fisherman has been the same confusion and controversy that has occurred in respect of a number of other industries; he has suffered in no small degree since confederation
The Budget-Mr. Pottier

by reason of this question of jurisdiction. When however we examine the developments since confederation, we find that the federal government has realized that the responsibility for taking care of the industry rests with the dominion government. For a long time there was a great deal of uncertainty as to the proprietary rights in fisheries, whether they belonged to the dominion or the provinces. In the British Columbia Fisheries Case and in other cases, it was decided that the fisheries rights in tidal waters belonged to the people of Canada as a whole rather than the dominion or the provinces. For that reason the federal government stated, in effect:	We will attend
only to regulation. The provincial governments, on the other hand, claimed that they had nothing to do with the matter. The result was that the fisherman found himself between the two jurisdictions, with no one agency to look after his welfare or to promote the development of the industry.
In considering what has happened since confederation, I think the federal government has admitted that responsibility for the fisheries rests with it. We find that by an award under the provisions of the Treaty of Washington, $4,500,000 was paid by the government of the United States for the right to take fish in the maritime provinces. The dominion government still retains that money; it is part of the consolidated revenue in the federal treasury.
A small item appears in the estimates each year for the development of the deep sea fisheries. Besides this, a commission was appointed by parliament to examine, in particular, into the maritime fisheries. If this government has no jurisdiction and no responsibility, why was the McLean commission appointed in 1927 to make a report to the federal government? I submit that when all is taken into consideration it must be realized that the dominion government have admitted responsibility; they have led the provinces to believe that they would assume the duty of developing 'the industry and enabling it to carry on. It may be of interest to note that in the last investigation, by the price spreads commission, the following reference was made to the maritime fisheries:
The investigation of the commission found a continuation of the conditions in 1927, though perhaps in a more accentuated form.
There is no doubt that in 1927 this industry was in jeopardy. It is not a question arising out of the depression; the very existence of the fishing industry is jeopardized. I submit therefore that this government must accept responsibility, that the development of the fisheries in the maritime provinces has become a matter of national emergency and national concern.

We of the maritimes had great hopes at the time of confederation. I think it was Joseph Howe who said that we were "leaving a country that had a past to join a country that had only a future." I am afraid that so far as the fishing industry is concerned, we have cause to feel that nothing has been gained. Canada uses only twenty-seven per cent of the production of the fisheries. We have to look to export trade for the balance, and I suggest that our national thought has been more to the development of our other primary products and industries.
The condition of this industry has been recognized, I believe, by all parties in this house. I quote from a speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) just previous to the last election, as reported by the Halifax Herald of October 4, 1935, while he was speaking at Bridgewater, in the constituency of the then minister of fisheries, Mr. Ernst:
Turning his attention to fisheries policies of the Conservative party, the Prime Minister declared an immediate survey of the entire industry was essential to spur the industry along a forward march of progress.
The remedies he suggested were:
"First: We must have better knowledge of the requirements of the people who buy our fish. . . .
Second:	trade commissioners should have
complete knowledge of the fisheries. . . .
Third: we must find out how most we can assist the fishermen. I confess I do not know. I tell you frankly. . . .
Fourth: we shall continue extensive advertising to make your fish better known."
So that the leader of the opposition, when he was Prime Minister, acknowledged and realized that the industry was in such peril that he recommended, an immediate survey, and he admitted he did not know what remedies should be applied to assist the individual fisherman.
Another indication of the condition of this industry is that the government of Nova Scotia on its own responsibility has been carrying on investigations. I suggest to hon. members that they read the Note on the Fisheries Industry issued by the Economic Council of the province of Nova Scotia in October and November 1936. I congratulate the premier of that province upon the interest he is showing in this matter.
There seems to be no question about the gravity of the situation. It is generally admitted by everyone who has any knowledge of the industry, including members of the various parties in this house, that the maritime fisherman is in a pitiful condition.
I realize that it would be unreasonable for me to ask for discrimination in his favour.

The Budget-Mr. Pottier
A country must be run by definite policies; otherwise everything will end in chaos. We cannot favour one against the other. I therefore propose briefly that we follow the policy adopted to take care of another primary producer in another part of Canada-the farmer of the west. I do not want any of my remarks to be interpreted as criticizing anything that has been done or is being done to help the western farmer. I refer to the details simply to indicate the policy that has been followed, and I ask that the same policy be applied in behalf of the fishermen of the maritime provinces.
Let us look at what has been happening in the last few years. We find that in 1934, chapter 36, there were amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act, an act passed some years ago to provide loans to farmers. I think it can be fairly said that in a large measure, at least, those amendments were introduced to take care of a condition that was developing in the Canadian west.
Going on to 1935, we find an act providing for a Canadian Wheat Board, chapter 53 of that year. The outstanding feature of that act was the power given to the government to buy and sell wheat. They were going a step further. They were going to buy the product in order to save the individual farmer, but that was not sufficient. In the same year they went still further, enacting a rehabilitation act for the benefit of the prairie provinces. What was the idea of that? It was to rehabilitate the individual farmer. We find that the government went yet another step and enacted the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, another measure to assist the farmer to carry on, helping him to the extent of enabling him to pay his bills in the amount that he could afford, the balance to be taken care of by compromise.
In connection with these policies with regard to wheat and rehabilitation, I would quote the remarks of the Prime Minister of that day (Mr. Bennett), to be found at page 3457 of Hansard of 1935. Referring to the necessity for the wheat board the right hon. gentleman gave the following explanation to parliament:
I think possibly I should say that once in this country we had a grain board brought about, of course, by the exigencies of the war. The situation at the present time, without going into the matter in detail, is that this country has not been able to market all its wheat...
The essential fact for us to recall is that the countries of Europe which during the war did not produce wheat found themselves dependent upon the countries which did increase their production, notably Canada, and that unfortunately for us for some strange reason, we did not realize that in 1925. 1926. 1927,
1928, 1929 and 1930 the countries of Europe had recovered their pre-war position-not only recovered it, but greatly strengthened it, and were supplying not only their own requirements but were also on an export basis.
Under these circumstances the position was a very simple one. The question was whether or not chaos should reign in respect to the largest industry we have, in point of value of exports, or whether something should be done to endeavour to save it from the chaotic condition prevailing. Something -was done.
In other words, the wheat board was brought into existence to save the individual wheat grower, and therefore to save the industry. For this purpose the government went into the market to buy and sell wheat. I submit that the policy adopted by the previous government was to help out the farmers of the west, because the industry had to be saved from the chaotic conditions then prevailing.
I pass next to the policy adopted by parliament when the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was passed. As indicated in Hansard of 1935 at page 2604, Hon. Mr. Weir, then Minister of Agriculture, on that occasion said:
Throughout the whole program it is our purpose to assist the farmers, and to demonstrate whether or not the people in these areas can continue to live there with only very little more moisture than they are now receiving. Our first aim is to do everything possible to make these people self-sustaining. Secondly, we must decide which areas are best suited for grain growing, which are best suited for ranching and the best way to handle those areas which are intermediate.
The basis of our work is a study of the people 'who have farmed in the district and who have made use of trees and dams and grasses and cultural methods, and then after an analysis and a summing up of what the experts so-called have felt were the most important factors in each ease, they will be able to place before a committee of farmers themselves in each province information that will be the basis on which all the work will be done.
The policy of helping the individual was being developed, and a further step in that direction was apparently the effort to restore confidence in the people and to help make them self-sustaining. The other day the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) 

I refer the house to Hansard, pages 779 and 780-when discussing an amendment to the rehabilitation bill recognized the policy laid* down by the previous government, and he went I submit a step still further. He hinted that the farmer might be moved from one district to another. An effort was to be made to find a proper home for him if necessary. I suggest that we have gone a long way in our endeavour to help this primary producer. First we have lent him money; secondly, we have erected' government institutions for the purchase and sale of his product; thirdly, we have passed the Farmers' Creditors
The Budget-Mr. Pottier

Arrangement Act to take care of his debts; fourthly, we have passed the rehabilitation act to rehabilitate ham; and in the last place we are getting ready to find a proper home for him to move into.
I am not saying for a moment that all this is wrong, nor do I envy the farmer for anything that has been done for him. All I am asking is that the fisherman in the general shuffle of policies should- be given a square deal.
I could go on to deal with other primary producers who have been helped by the policies of the government but time does not permit. I do not suggest that the farmer has been singled out for special treatment to the exclusion of the fisherman in particular. But let us see what has been done for the fisherman. In 1935 we passed a fisherman's loan act for the benefit of fishermen, but very few loans have been made under it, although many people in my constituency have asked me to assist and recommend them for loans. I suggest that the act should be amended to make loans possible not only on house mortgages but on the security of fishermen's equipment.
In the maritimes there are 41,000 fishermen representing a dependent- population of about 200,000, and I suggest to the government that a maritime provinces fisheries rehabilitation act be passed- for the maritime provinces to provide machinery and money so as to accomplish, at any rate in part, the following: 1. A survey of the industry; 2. provision for machinery for the proper equipment of the fishermen; 3. an improvement in conditions so as to give the individual fisherman a better return for his labour; 4. the provision of fishermen's emergency relief, when required; and 5, the bringing about of better conditions that will save the industry from the chaotic conditions that now prevail.
I have read several times the words of the Hon. George Brown spoken on one occasion at Quebec. He said:
It may be that some among us will yet live to see the day when as a result of this measure a great and powerful people may have grown up on these lands-when the boundless forests all around us shall have given way to smiling fields and thriving towns, and when one united government under the British flag shall extend from shore to shore.
I am convinced th-at unless something is done in the ways I have indicated we shall have no thriving towns and smiling fields on the shores of the maritime provinces, but
fMr. Pottier.]
instead villages gone and forgotten with cellars remaining only as gaping monuments of days gone by.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A hundred years ago Mal-thus said that no man had any right to support from any quarter except his parents. And in 1931 the then Prime Minister said in this house that no one should be allowed to perish.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member was
asking a question I believe I would say that in dealing with the depression I think I said the government would not permit any man in the country to be without food, shelter, or clothing. My memory is that that was the sense of it, anyway.

The Budget-Mr. Moore

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, that was my memory
of it, and there was no objection. We who then sat on the other side of the house raised no objection. As I listened to-day to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier) who just preceded me I could not help thinking of those statements, as he talked about the liabilities of the country and the responsibility of the Minister of Finance to the fishermen. We have come to a new era, which means among other things that debtor countries cannot afford to risk specialization.
After citing the figures of agricultural income for representative countries, the League Survey of 1934-35 concludes:
It is clear that the fall in agricultural income was least in those countries where farming is a sheltered industry producing mainly for the home market, greater in those countries which produced manufactured food products such as meat and dairy produce, and greatest on those, such as Canada and Hungary, which exported mainly grains and vegetable raw material.
I believe we should lay aside some of our preconceived theories. I believe we should think of the great lessons of the depression and of the need for a balanced economy. The leader of the opposition has just given us a statement of what he promised those who were down and out. Well, you have to draw upon the Minister of Finance, you have to draw upon the treasury, not only of the dominion but of the provinces. I am glad to say that balances look better these days- the last two or three days, at any rate. But there does come a time when the supply dries up. There does come a time when idleness eats into the hearts of men. Then you have a social problem, and there comes a time when the problem is no longer economic, when politicians must ask themselves how they are going to put these people to work.
Our tariffs set out our economic boundaries. We have to think very carefully as to the future relation of our foreign and domestic trade. I should like very much to have gone into some of the details-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go ahead.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -but I do not want to take too much of the time of the house. Particularly should I like to speak about wheat. I have an idea-and I may be quite wrong- that the preference on wheat under the Ottawa agreements of 1932 was the bait for the pact. I think the then prime minister rather hinted at it, and I have the idea that this government has been attracted by the idea of a preference on wheat.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sir Wilfrid was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: By a free market for it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You got a preference for it, but of what use is that preference? Am I to understand that it is of some use, or that it is of no use?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is arguable; a free market is certainly valuable.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, let me quote the argument of a celebrated economist. Possibly the leader of the opposition will remember the statement to which I am about to refer. I am quoting Doctor Benham, who made this statement at a conference in Milan just prior to the Ottawa conference of 1932:
Canada and Australia together export more wheat than Great Britain consumes. What does that mean? Supposing Great Britain said: We will put on a tariff of 100 per cent or 1,000 per cent, or we will prohibit all foreign wheat, it would not help the Canadians and Australians one little bit as long as they competed with one another, because Canada and Australia together produce more wheat than Great Britain consumes. In any case, some of the wheat would have to be sold outside, and if a Canadian producer can get a little more in England than he can get somewhere else, then he will send his wheat to England, and therefore the price of Canadian and Australian wheat in England would be kept down at the world level.
Then Doctor Benham winds up by saying:
For those tw-o reasons I see nothing important which will be done at Ottawa.
I am inclined to think nothing very important to our advantage was done in 1932, and I hold the same view to-d'ay.
Now I go further and say that I believe every government has mandates from the people. I think the present government had two or three of them, the first of which was to restore responsible government-what we believe was responsible government,-and in my opinion they have not done it. Mandate number two was to provide profitable jobs for Canadians. We all know whether they have or have not done that. Then there is a third mandate, one which confronts every government, and that which I believe is an important one, namely good relations within the empire and without. I wonder if an imperial economic pact is designed to bring good relations within the empire? I do not wish to say anything against the right hon. gentleman who was the prime minister in 1932, but when he was dealing with Mr. Baldwin it seems to me both of them had some cards up their sleeves that were not altogether disclosed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not familiar with cards; I do not understand them.
The Budget-Mr. Moore

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, there are all kinds of cards. We know that the mother country is a wonderful thing, and I have every respect for it; but mother is a sharp trader.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I agree with that, at any rate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And the Minister of Finance agrees. When they came here with their experts, and filled the Chateau to overflowing, they came after having arranged to subsidize the production of wheat in Great Britain. Of course that was known to the then prime minister of Canada. That had two effects, and I want hon. members to think of them, because the condition still exists. The first effect was to increase the quantity of wheat. When the arrangement was put into operation Great Britain was producing only about fifteen per cent of its supply of wheat; the last records show that they now produce about twenty-five per cent. There is another effect. They take part of that subsidy from the Canadian wheat grower through an excise tax on flour. The proceeds of that tax are distributed to their own wheat growers. That is their business, but what about our business? I wonder what the Englishman would say if we put a tax on all textiles coming in from the United Kingdom and distributed it to our small mills or, if you prefer, to our homespun textile industry? I wonder if the Englishman would think we were guilty of sharp practice?	I wonder if he would think
that we were mitigating to some extent the reductions in tariff that were given? The old country provided-I think the prime minister of the day slipped up a bit-against any combination on our part that would destroy or hold back the sale of wheat in England at world prices. That is the argument Doctor Benham used.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) says he is not accustomed to cards, but he appears to 'have had one up his Sleeve. He said he would fix the world price by having a controlled price. I suppose that was all in the game. But Great Britain also had a card uip her sleeve. There is more than one way of providing a preference. The Minister of Finance will remember the treaty made with the Argentine in 1933, immediately after the other agreements went into effect. Under that treaty provision was made for a loan, which really was t'he equivalent of a preference, to assist in the exportation of agricultural products, including wheat, from the Argentine to the United Kingdom.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And the export of machinery from England.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. I shall not give a lot of statistics as to what happened, but I should like to quote one statement made before the imperial economic committee in 1936:
During the period under review the United Kingdom has been a steady purchaser of cereals. Although the United Kingdom taxed foreign wheat 2s. per quarter late in 1932 as a result of the Ottawa agreements, imports of foreign wheat have increased each year since then, while imports from the empire have fallen in 1934 and 1935.
We could go on and talk of the drought in western Canada, but it must be remembered that they had a serious drought in the Argentine. It is only my own opinion, but when everything is considered I doubt the value of a preference on wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But you admit the value of a free market?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was always free except during the South African war.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not want anyone to think that I am prejudiced against trade with Great Britain. I think sometimes we politicians on both sides of the 'house are the object of suspicions which we do not deserve. I want to quote a word or two by some political philosophers as to the political effect of the Ottawa agreements. In 1933, immediately after the agreements had been effected, there wias a meeting of the International Institute of Intellectual Cooperation. This meeting was held in London, and if we are ever to find political philosophers surely they should be found at a convention of the International Institute of Intellectual Cooperation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Its headquarters are in Paris.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a branch of the league of nations. Professor Jacob Viner, of Chicago, was there. I understand that this gentleman used to be a Canadian, at least a British subject. He said:
I feel convinced there is no future for the British Empire on the basis of quid pro quo imperialism. If they try systematically to make mutual profit out of their empire, they will find that Britishers are too good bargainers to remain good friends. That is a matter which used of right to be of concern to me. Perhaps I should not longer speak on such questions. They are perhaps private matters.
Let .us have an Englishman's view. I quote Professor Bailey, of London university, who said:
Nothing in the history of the British commonwealth of nations is more likely to disrupt the association between the various partners than the recently concluded Ottawa agreements.

The Budget-Mr. Moore
Professor Coabman, who was in the chair, had this to say:
The outlook was dark in those days and it was natural, in view of the great unemployment here and in Canada, that the minds of men should be dominated by this short term policy of trade agreements and so on.
We are now asked to make, shall I say, a permanent arrangement. We are being asked to take the second step in economic imperialism. Somehow I think that we within the British Empire will be able to get along. We are pretty good friends, but the Ottawa agreements have a direct effect on the world's present hazardous position. There is no doubt about that. Professor Von Beckerath, who was speaking for Germany, had this to say at the same conference:
Although the Ottawa agreements may be consonant with the Zeitgeist, we cannot at the same time believe them to be objectively good. The interesting argument was put forward that in the long run the whole world economic order must profit by a procedure by which the economic situation and productivity within the realm of the British Empire gets better. Under certain conditions that is a small consolation for certain countries' who are only interested in making sure of their share.
And he continued:
Economists should bear these factors in mind when planning a new economic world order. There are members of that world order who are sick, and one cannot, without causing great harm in the long run, act on the assumption that all the members are strong and well when such a condition does not exist.
I was interested the other day in the little passage at arms as to who had been the better essayist, the man who wrote the agreements of 1932 or the man who wrote the agreement of 1937, on the question whether economic imperialism or the pact of 1932 or the pact of 1937 will lead to greater world trade, and I was interested in this statement in the London Economist, which journal, I think everybody will admit, is practically the organ of international liberalism:
The British government, acting within the letter of the most-favoured-nation clause but scarcely within its spirit, concluded the Ottawa agreements, which effectively imposed fresh handicaps on the trade of many countries with Britain and her dominions and empire. The inevitable reaction to the Ottawa gesture, and to the new British tariff accompanying it, was that the countries most affected proceeded to strengthen their own barriers. Ottawa had, in fact, quite the opposite effect to that which Mr. Baldwin declared to be its intention- namely, to loosen the shackles of world trade.
Let hon. members carry their minds back to world conditions in 1932. They will remember that Japan was stretching out her hands for a new empire in Asia. They will remember the bold steps that were taken,
and the defiance of the League of Nations. Those who keep in touch with the publication Pacific Affairs will remember that the Japanese stated in effect: We are going to do as Britain has done. It is only a step to trace the movement to Italy and on to Germany, and then to remember that Ottawa led the way. I have no desire to exaggerate, and when I make a statement of that kind I want to give some tangible evidence. If hon. members will turn up the League of Nations Survey for 1934-35 they will find that it refers to the conference that was held in Paris in 1935 to tighten the bonds of the French empire, and the League's observers say that that conference was called a "French Ottawa." The league observers go on to relate the trade agreements in which the nations of the world sought to protect themselves from the consequences of our new imperialism, and they wind up with this conclusion:
The list of these agreements is very long and as they follow each other in rapid succession, their practical effect is not only restrictive of trade but leads irresistibly to a greater degree of state control.
And may I add, war. You have to-day a division of the nations, and you say it is socialist, fascist and liberal. Well, Russia is all for peace. We of the British Empire are all for peace. The United States is for peace. It is the "have-nots" that are for war. When we made a preferential pact, though we had the old preference before, we have affected the psychology of nations. It is all very well to say, and I have no doubt the Minister of Finance will say, that every nation-Germany, Italy and the rest-is able to buy our wheat on a free market; they do not need to put tariffs against it. Quite true, but they have to have means of payment, and we have given Great Britain, their industrial rival, a preference in the means of payment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have done so for forty years.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As I suggested a little while ago, when the whole empire is brought together, a psychological effect is produced different from that resulting from individual preferences under the old arrangement made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The other dominions gave preferences.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, the others gave preferences too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For many years.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I follow that thought? You had a different condition after the war. Before the war London was the world's banker,
i662
The Budget-Mr. Moore

lending money all over the globe, and half of it to foreign countries. When, in 1932, Great Britain and the dominions came together, a very different condition existed. Great Britain had lost some of her credit. The United States, the world's new banker, would not allow the peoples to pay their debts in goods. In the old days Canada and the dominions provided practically an open door for immigration, but after the war that door was closed. That was the atmosphere in which the Ottawa agreements were devised and which we to-day are asked, I take it, to perpetuate. I do not feel that I can support them. I do not believe that the Canadian people as a whole have realized the responsibility those agreements entail. I doubt whether from the debate a few days ago this house is prepared to defend a pact of economic imperialism. But surely we cannot leave others to defend the trade routes for which we have bargained! We cannot be a party to economic imperialism and then run away from its defence! We cannot contribute to the cause of war and then run away from war.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the opening session of this parliament, somewhat over a year ago, I told a number of Liberal members, many of whom were then entering the house for the first time, that they had a magnificent opportunity to render a great service to Canada, but I wondered whether sooner or later they would not find that their individual convictions conflicted with party expediency, and whether in all probability the latter would not prevail. At that time I assured the government that if they would use their unparalleled majority to remedy some of the domestic problems and grievances and injustices that were noticeably prevalent I would support them. We are now, Mr. Speaker, approaching the end of the second session, and we are justified in asking this question: Has the government, with its unequalled opportunity and its huge majority, been true to the confidence imposed in it by the people? In other words, is it keeping faith? The views I shall express this afternoon will be offered rather in a spirit of warning than of condemnation, but I wish to call attention to certain things which in my opinion should engage the attention of parliament. In doing so I say to the minister at once that any apparent criticism I offer is not directed at him personally, because 1 do recognize that he is an able administrator of his department. I believe he has devoted his strength and energy to the discharge of his duties. But having said that, I do not

think it necessarily follows that I must agree with the policies he has enunciated on behalf of the governmeirt or with all that he has said in the name of the government in the course of his budget. Before I proceed let me express to my hon. friend who has just taken his seat, the member for Ontario (Mr. Moore), my admiration of the manner in which he always presents his thoughts. A little later I have some remarks to make on the British agreement and I will reserve until then anything I have to say to him. I shall probably refer to his remarks then. I hope therefore he will not think I am neglecting him at the moment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The annual budget, I presume, is intended to give to parliament a broad picture of the country's economic condition and to indicate policies for the removal of such grievances as may exist. This budget, I submit with all due respect to the minister, was perhaps the longest, and apart from the presentation of the British agreement, about as barren a budget as any I have listened to in twenty-six years-not barren perhaps of reports of conditions, which reports were most admirably given, but barren of real remedies for internal or domestic problems which I know are agitating the minds not only of members opposing the government but of members sitting on the other side.
Let me invite hon. members, particularly my Liberal friends, to put to themselves a few pertinent questions. What hope is offered in this budget to the unemployed toilers of the country? What assurances are there to the struggling farmers of relief from exploitation? What solace is there to the harassed business man who finds himself little more than a tax collecting agency for the government? Business men in this house know very well that this description of the average modern business man is perhaps as nearly correct as any description could be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh no.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister says "Oh no," but I have talked with scores and scores of business men who, with the innumerable reports, tax schedules and so on, which they are obliged to make out, are little more than tax collecting agencies for the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Their income tax returns do not show it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The other day I was talking to a prominent business man who told me that his business had increased over fifty per cent in 1936, but that he had made less

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
and had worked harder for it; and he gave as the reason that increased taxation and harassing measures imposed by provincial, municipal and dominion governments were occupying the time and attention of the staff to the exclusion of the business of the company.
What answer is given to the repeated declarations of certain of the provinces that they cannot carry on the responsibilities placed upon them in social services and other lines, the relief of unemployment and all these other problems, with the revenues they are able to collect at the present time? That problem is before parliament; it is before the government; and nothing in this budget indicates a policy that will afford relief. I ask: What does the government propose to do about the continuing national railways deficit? And again we are bound to say that the budget gives us no answer.
I do not intend to deal with unemployment or the devastating relief charges, because they have been debated in the house for the last week. I will say nothing in that regard except this, that there is no current policy of the government that would indicate any permanent remedy for this condition of unemployment, unless perhaps it is contained in the plaintive cry of the government for wider markets. To that I shall return a little later.
Let me turn now to the British agreement. The hon. member for Ontario, who is so well qualified to discuss matters of this kind, not only by reason of his long study of these subjects but also because of his experience as chairman of the tariff board for a number of years, takes exception to the British agreement. I should like to call to his attention one set of facts which he seems to have overlooked. He referred to the historic background of 1932, but if you want to find what really made necessary the Ottawa agreements you have to go back ten years beyond that and follow up step by step the tendency of Italy, Germany and other European countries, which previously had been excellent markets for Canadian goods but which virtually closed their doors to Canadian products, particularly wheat, dairy produce, meat and other products of the farm. Italy raised its duty on wheat from free to something like 97 cents a bushel; Germany raised its duty to 87 and then to 90 cents and then to $1 a bushel. Other countries did the same, and Canada was confronted in 1932-in fact prior to that year-with markets which had been hers for years being gradually closed to her. That was the condition that obtained at that time. When therefore Canada entered into these agreements there was more justification for them than was indicated in 31111-105
the very able address by the hon. member for Ontario. I can quite appreciate the broad philosophical view which the hon. member takes; but unfortunately we are not dealing at this time, or indeed at any time, with countries who direct their financial policies on broad philosophical lines. The unfortunate part is that we are dealing with countries that erect tariffs and impose quotas and inhibitions of various kinds; and these things were done before Canada took action at all. And because of these things Canada, other dominions of the empire and the mother country, deemed it necessary to enter into these agreements.

speechtext:
Yes; I recall my hon. friend having said that. This agreement which the minister has introduced in the budget is the one and only justification for the presentation of the budget, apart from a review of conditions. The government is to be congratulated in my opinion on securing an extension of the agreement for a further period of three years, because the agreement in essence is the same as the preceding one, and what the minister has done is to ensure a continuity of the trade expansion achieved so remarkably under the old agreement. I congratulate the government on having secured an extension of this agreement for a period of three years. It is not my intention to discuss the agreement, because when we come to the committee stage there may be items which will require scrutiny and debate. On the whole I agree with the agreement. It marks, I believe, the sensible abandonment by the government of the impossible stand taken by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in 1932. He said that if and when the Liberal party came into office the first thing it would do would be to repeal, rescind and abandon these agreements, and I say that the abandonment of that position by the Liberal party and the Liberal government is a matter of congratulation to the government. It displays a degree of common sense for which I think they should be commended.
I am not going to say more about the agreement, because there are other subjects with which I wish to deal. The government, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), and I believe the Liberal party, attach great importance to external trade. I warned them last year, and I warn them again, that in external trade we are not going to find the

The Budget-Mr. Stevens

solution for the domestic problems of Canada. I am not belittling external trade; I think it is a splendid thing if we can extend our trade, and I know that every government, no matter 'how it might be composed, certainly would do its best to extend our trade with foreign countries. In his budget speech, however, the minister 'had this to say-I invite the attention of the house to his words, and after reading them I propose to review them very briefly:
This expansion of our foreign commerce of course reflects in part the improvement in world conditions. . . . But that is by no means the whole story ... it is not unreasonable to interpret this as clear evidence of the success of the governments trade policies.
Those are the words of the minister. Here he takes his stand; here is the justification for the policies of the government. I have no doubt that the minister invites analysis and criticism, so let us examine the matter.
The minister tells us that the increase of exports in 1936 over 1935 was $189,920,000, and I recall that when the minister made that announcement there were loud cheers from the party supporting the government. If, as the minister says, credit is due the government for that increase in exports, then I suppose the government would not object if we laid at their door responsibility for any diminution in trade or any decrease in exports. I think the responsibility must rest with them in the latter case if they choose to accept credit for the former. Let us examine these increases in exports. It is easy and simple to do.
Among the principal increases we find that the export of alcoholic beverages increased by $10,000,000. Well, I am quite prepared to say that government policy was responsible for that; let them have the credit. But next we find an increase of $89,750,000 in the export of wheat. There was no government policy responsible in that case. It was the result of a world drought condition, plus a war scare, plus a surplus that had been accumulated during the regime of a Tory government. What was a tragedy last year is today a great boon to the country, and is announced in the budget as part of the great surplus of exports. But that would not have been possible if that unfortunate accumulation had not been there; so certainly that was not diue to any policy of this government.
The next large item of increased exports is in wood products, amounting to $35,000,000, and if you want the reason for the steadily increasing export of wood products in recent years you must turn to the Ottawa agreements.

Now I turn to some other large items of increased exports:
Scrap iron	$1,266,000
Zinc	 1,100,000
Copper	 7.000.000
Nickel	 8,300.000
Lead	 3,250,000
In these five classes of metals we have an increase of about S21,000,000, every particle of which was due to the war scare in Europe, and not to government policy. The minister said the increase of exports was partly due to good policy, and partly due to good luck. I would say it was stark tragedy, international insanity, that was the reason for this great stimulation in the export of these metals. For seven, eight or nine da)'s we debated the question of defence; member after member called to the attention of the house the tragedy of this war scare-and that is what was responsible for this increase.
Our exports increased by $189,900,000 as compared with 1935, and these three items I have named, wheat, lumber and metals, with which government policy had nothing to do, account for $145,000,000 of that increase. I do not wish to take away from the minister or the government any comfort they can get out of the improved times, but it is well for the house to look at these figures and to realize that there is nothing very stable or secure in them. If the thing we all profess to desire, a condition of mind that would engender peace, could be brought about in the world, much of this trade would vanish overnight. If tomorrow the nations of the world were assured that there was no danger of war, prices of metal and our exports of metal would fall in a tragic way. So would the price of wheat and the exports of wheat, and we might say the same of other commodities. Thus, Mr. Speaker, when we look at the improved conditions and analyze the figures, we must come to the conclusion that not very much of the improvement is due to government policy.
Now let me turn to the other side of the picture. A moment ago I suggested that if the government should receive credit for increases. it must accept responsibility for decreases. What about these decreases? In the export of motor trucks the decrease was $1,100,000, and in the export of passenger cars $1,600,000; or a total decrease of S2,700,000 in the export of automobiles, representing 8,760 vehicles. That was in the calendar year 1936, as against 1935. Again I ask if the government is prepared to take responsibility for that.
Then let us take fruits, which concern a very substantial section of this country. The diminution in the export of fruits amounts to

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
$4,230,000. In exports of apples the decrease was $3,850,000; in other fresh fruits $265,000; and in canned fruits $245,000. Then take shingles, an important item to the province of British Columbia. These exports have fallen off by $1,200,000. There has been a decrease in the exports of sausage casings amounting to $185,000, and in processed milk of $366,000. In patent leather the decrease has been $400,000; in malt. S500.000; in electric vacuum cleaners, $400,000; in sewing machines, $500,000; in soap. $400,000, and in oats, $2,140,000. These, Mr. Speaker, are decreases in exports, and again I ask if the government is responsible for these decreases. Why does not the minister give us an analysis of the decreases?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, the government sold some wheat. Last year on the floor of this house we listened to the most bitter condemnation of the wheat policy of the previous administration, under which that accumulation of wheat took place, and if it had not been for that accumulation the minister would not have had the wheat to export.
Now let us come to the subject so ably discussed a few moments ago by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier), who made an appeal to the minister. Let me put this to the minister: Is the policy of the government responsible for the decrease in the exports of fish? Those decreases were as follows:
Dried codfish	$500,000
Herring	 150,000
Pickled mackerel	 40,000
Dry salt salmon	 90,000
Pickled salmon	 177,000
Canned lobster	 195,000
Canned salmon	 1,030,000
Once again I ask the minister, who is responsible for those decreases? Let me take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare on his very able speech, the preparation of which must have required a great deal of time and thought. I want to say to the hon. member that one of the problems of the fishing industry, and one of the root causes of distress among the fishermen, lies in the control of the distribution of fish by the National Fish Company. That is where the trouble lies. Will this government do anything in regard to it? I am warning this government and hon. members from Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces, where large fisheries exist, that they will find a major cause of their trouble in regard to fisheries in the overbearing and dictatorial power exercised by the great distributing companies, chiefly the National Fish Company. That is where the trouble lies, and that is where we must correct the trouble. I asked the president of that company, when he appeared before a parliamentary committee some two years ago, if, somewhere between the half cent a pound paid to the fishermen and the twenty to thirty cents a pound for which the fish were sold, another half cent could not be found for the fishermen, and he said it could not. All we have to do is pause for a moment and ask ourselves in this parliament if we are helpless to find the fishermen another half cent a pound. I was in the little town of Sackville, I think it was, though I am not quite sure- at any rate it was close to the bay of Fundy, in the southern part of New Brunswick-[DOT] when a fisherman brought in five hundred pounds of the finest haddock one could wish to see. I wonder if hon members will believe me when I tell them what that man received for that five hundred pounds of fish. I was there that day, and was told by the man personally that he received one dollar, or one-fifth of a cent per pound. The hon. member for Sheliburne-Yarmouth-Clare knows, as other hon. members know, that in the
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

speechtext: Fifteen.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thought it was more than that, but fifteen is a fairly large number. Fifteen Liberal members stood in their places and denounced the defence policy; then, like sheep, they walked up and voted for the very policy they had denounced. There is only one weapon left to a member of parliament, only one way in which he can express his objection ito anything; that is by his vote, and I sat here and saw that spectacle go on day after day. Members made magnificent, interesting speeches in which they presented their views ably and gave cogent reasons for the stand they were taking; then they declared by itheir vote their unswerving support of the government. Why? Well, they know better than I do, but speaking in a general way I know the reason is the fear of losing the patronage which goes to supporters of the government. This inglorious position in which parliament finds itself is due largely to the failure of parliament to occupy the field that has been given it under the British North America Act. I said that two years ago; I

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
repeat it to-day. Parliament is not occupying the field it was given under the British North America Act. Parliament is not and has not been discharging the powers it rightfully enjoys. It will not and it is not applying those powers to the remedy of public grievances in the country. Parliament is perishing slowly but surely from inertia and ineptitude. We play the game of politics, but we do not play the game with the people.
Let us look at the privy council decisions. Only one measure came through the reference to that body, and I pause to say that those references never should have been made- never. The only way properly to test a law is to put it into operation, with the force and influence of the government behind it. Then let a citizen challenge t'he law in the courts on its merits. But what is the sense, where is the courage, in taking a measure before it is given am opportunity to operate, and placing it before the courts, saying "Please tell us, have we done right or have we done wrong?" The basis of consideration under those circumstances is wholly technical and constitutional-not upon the merits, or upon a consideration of whether the law is applied correctly.
In spite of all that, one measure survived, the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act, which provided for the setting up of a tribunal before which those having grievances in connection with trade practices might appear. I shall not go into details, but I must say it has never yet been given a chance to operate. In the first place, administration of the act was given to the tariff board, a body already overwhelmed with duties. When the present government took office they referred the measures to the courts, and since that nothing has been done. Not even the prosecutor has been appointed, an officer of the crown who was to administer those obscure laws already on the statute books, but which business men and others hesitate to invoke.
Some time ago a prominent business man drew to my attention a flagrant violation of the criminal code in connection with false advertising. There was no question as to the falsity of the advertising. He said, "Well, how can we have the act enforced? I have asked the Attorney General, and he does not take any interest in it." I am not sure whether he said he had consulted the Department of Justice. I said to him, "Lay the information yourself." But he replied, "Oh, no, I cannot lay the information." He did not want to do it, and as a matter of fact he should not be asked to do it. The measure provides for the appointment of an officer
to prosecute on behalf of the public in the event of violation of a law such as that respecting false advertising, which has been in the criminal code for years, but which has had nobody to enforce it. There is law dealing with false advertising, and deceiving or defrauding the public. Can the government do anything to correct that? Of course they can. What action is being taken? Concluding that part of my remarks, I say that if in the next two years parliament does not produce some practical results in the correction of grievances within Canada, then Canada is heading for disintegration and dissolution. Some may think that is strong language, but I warn the house that there is a deep-rooted dissatisfaction throughout Canada with the manner in which our affairs are handled under the so-called constitution.
Let me now turn to another subject. May I ask the minister this direct question: What does he intend to do about the railway deficit? Here is what he says:
I shall be greatly disappointed if we cannot keep our total deficit for 1937-38 within the limit represented by the net cash deficit of the Canadian National Railway System.
And I recall that that was greeted with cheers. What a thing to put before the taxpayers of Canada-we hope next year to restrict the deficit within what we are going to lose on the Canadian National Railways. That was a very graceful way of evading a very difficult question.
It is not as if we did not have information about the matter, because we have had most intensive investigations of the railway problem. We have had engineers' reports, expert opinions, traffic surveys, royal commissions, special committees of parliament, and standing committees of parliament, for twenty years to my knowledge. Since 1017 and the Drayton-Acworth report we have gone on year after year, accumulating data and information of all kinds until we have it by the ton-literally, Mr. Speaker, by the ton -in the archives of parliament. It is all there, available for the use of parliament. What are we doing about it?-just nothing; nothing.
Let me now examine some of the reports. I have the Drayton-Acworth report and the report of the Duff commission before me, but I shall not go into them in detail. I shall not read them, because anyone who wishes to may read them.
I shall be content with pointing out only one or two points. Some of the recommendations of the Drayton-Acworth report were adopted, thereby giving birth to the Canadian National railways. But its most vital recommendations
166S
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

were ignored, and because of that Canada has a railway problem. Those recommendations were that the railways were to be operated by trustees-I am talking about twenty years ago. They were to be operated upon a commercial basis, and were to be undisturbed politically. The trustees were to be nonpolitical, permanent and self-perpetuating. They were to be given the widest powers in the management of the property. It is the disregard of these recommendations which has been the chief cause of the deficit and our dilemma in connection with our railways. They have been subjected to political interference; no one can deny that. Let us be frank; let us state frankly what we know. We know they have been subject to political interference. We know that political lines were bought; I know it, other hon. members know it. We know, too, that political branch lines costing scores of millions of dollars were built; we know that. We know that there was political interference with the managements; we cannot deny that. No man can deny it. Yet these were the very things against which the Drayton-Acworth report of twenty years ago warned parliament and the people of [DOT]Canada.
What did the Duff report say? Speaking Pf the Drayton-Acworth report made fifteen years previously, the Duff commission made these observations in 1932:
The recommendations were designed to provide safeguards against political interference but-
And this is the finding of the Duff commission :
-the government declined to follow the plan of organization recommended by the commission.
Then they go on to show what the results have been. In other words, this parliament, you and I, stand convicted before the people of Canada of having failed to carry out the expert advice given to us, and particularly in connection with the one point of political interference, which has been the nemesis of the Canadian National railways from its very inception. The Duff commission made recommendations among which were emancipation from political influence, elimination of duplication, cooperation between the two systems, and economies. They proposed to achieve these objectives by the appointment of three trustees, to be appointed from a panel named by themselves. Then, there was to be an arbitral tribunal to adjudicate in connection with disputes between the two systems. In part, that was put into law in 1933.
But once again politics wrecked the recommendations of that commission. Once more we are floundering in a sea of prejudice and

partisanship. We have no chart, no compass; this parliament is just drifting so far as the railway problem is concerned. Yet this problem is the source of the greatest proportion of our deficits. It is the most serious problem, and has been so declared over and over again, with which Canada is confronted. Yet we are drifting along just as we have drifted for twenty years-and we expect the country to have confidence in parliament! I would not presume to say that I have a remedy or a solution for this problem, but there are a few suggestions I should like to make.
