speechtext:
The two previous speakers took ten minutes more; I have only a few further sentences in connection with this railway problem. I would suggest, first, that we agree in both houses of parliament to drop politics when we are discussing the railway problem. That is a real foundation upon which we might hope to build something of value. Second, I would suggest that we refer all existing data to three committees, made up of senators and members of parliament-[DOT] one committee to report on coordination, another to report on the rights of labour, and the third to report on the elimination of political interference and influence. Then I suggest that, we hold a special session of parliament this autumn for the exclusive purpose of discussing and dealing with the railway problem and receiving the reports of these committees.
I have this further suggestion to make, one which has been in my mind for many years but which I have never uttered as I felt it was more within the realm of experts and I feared to tread therein. I have been in the house twenty years, and year after year this railwaj' problem comes up and nothing is done. I am going to make this further suggestion. There is not a single transcontinental railway in the United States. Let hon. members get that. Canada should be divided into three zones for transportation purposes, one taking in Fort William to the coast; another taking in the great central areas of Ontario and Quebec, as far east as Quebec or Riviere du Loup; and the third taking in the maritime provinces. The maritime provinces have their confederation problems which are entitled to consideration. The great central provinces have their dense traffic problems, and the west has its wheat and farm products movements and other problems peculiar to that part of the country. Each of these zones

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
ought to be administered from a central point within itself, and inter-zone traffic arrangements made just as they are made in the United States.
With a system of that kind I believe we could 'bring the railway problem of Canada within the ambit of the understanding of a board of directors or a group of individuals. Quite frankly I question whether any one mind or any one board is capable of fully understanding and grasping the problems of either the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific from Halifax to Vancouver. I contend that if parliament and the country would address themselves to this problem and take advantage of the information within our archives, a solution could be found.
Before I take my seat let me say one word in conclusion. In order that a democracy may succeed, it must be founded upon justice and equity within the state. Hon. members know that there are serious grievances which remain uncured. Apparently there is no possibility of correction by parliament, and until we as a parliament address ourselves to the correction of these iniquities, we cannot hope to retain the confidence and respect of the people of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I should like to join those who have already congratulated the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon his excellent presentation of the budget. There are some things in the budget I like and there are some I dislike. I dislike exceedingly both the sales tax and the sugar tax, but I do not propose to discuss them this afternoon. I think we have had a most .profitable discussion to-day The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore) brought a refreshing air of reality into the debate. We may not agree with his philosophical fundamentals, we may not agree with his conclusions, but at least we can admit that he has given this house food for thought. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) has done the same thing in a somewhat different manner.
I would point out that while the hon. member for Ontario was speaking, the evening editions of the local newspapers were delivered in the chamber. One of the statements appearing therein bears out what the hon. member said, that the Ottawa agreements might have repercussions which were not foreseen by some who supported the last agreements. We read in the press that the Australian Minister of Trade has resigned. The article continues:
Canada found it impossible to agree to concessions of such magnitude, it was understood. The Canadian argument was that the balance
of trade in Canada's favour was a natural one, largely because Canadian industry had developed to a point at which it was able to provide cheaply and efficiently a large range of manufactures which Australia required.
The commercial situation is thus set out in a few words. Every nation including this dominion is ready to sell but is not ready to buy.
The budget speech contains only a brief reference to a matter which I wish to discuss. The minister said that it was a matter for congratulation that a liability of amazing proportions in our national finances had been removed. He referred specifically to the accumulation of wheat which in a few short months had turned from a great liability into an asset of national importance.
Last evening the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made what I thought was an extraordinary and rather weak defence of the government's policy in relation to the marketing of wheat. The minister devoted considerable time to a comparison of prices in widely dissimilar periods during past years. He paid no attention to the point made this afternoon by the hon. member for Ontario, that during those years there had been tremendous increases in both acreage and production not only in the four great wheat producing countries but also in the importing countries. The result was that during that period a glut occurred. He forgot to mention, of course, that this accumulation began under the previous Liberal administration, whose failure to implement their own tariff policies and the wheat board legislation of 1922 was, I believe, in no small measure responsible for the accumulations. The failure to implement the wheat board legislation led, in 1923 and 1924, the years to which the minister referred, to the formation of the second best thing to a wheat board from the point of view of the western farmer-the Canadian pools. The minister said last evening, at page 1631 of Hansard:
The question of how wheat is to be marketed is of great importance to all the people of Canada, but it is of particular importance to the people who produce it.
That, I might say, is the reason why the the government's disregard of the wishes of the producers is very keenly resented throughout western Canada. The efforts of our farmers over a period of at least thirty years to create and to own their own marketing facilities prove conclusively that thieir hope of getting equitable prices for theiir products was through the establishment of their own marketing organization rather than in risking alternately high and1 low prices-mainly low prices-on a purely speculative market. It is this effort which the farmers of the west
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

believe the attitude and the policy of the government and the present wheat board have very largely nullified. The minister said, at page 1632 of Hansard:
The person who buys the wheat is concerned only with the difference between the price at which he buys and the price at which he is able to sell.
Quite so, and that of course is the attitude of the trader, and of the middleman into whose hands, we believe, the government has played during the past eighteen months or so; for the bigger the difference between those two prices, the greater the profit to the speculator. I recommend to hon. members that they read the resolutions that were passed by western farmers during August and September last. They will find that those resolutions were more concerned with the method of marketing, the retention of the wheat board, than with a minimum price. Again may I repeat, in the words of the minister:
The question of how wheat is to be marketed is of great importance to...the people who produce it.
Knowing this, I rather admire the courage of the minister, who last night, by inference at least, condemned the pools and their policies, and in effect gave his approval to the grain exchange method of marketing the farmers' crop. The minister contended, at page 1633 of Hansard, that the farmers are obtaining to-day:
...the highest price for wheat.. .since the beginning of the stabilization activities of Mr. McFarland.
Are the farmers getting that price or are the speculators getting it? If the speculators are getting it, I should like to know why they should be allowed to do so. Look at the world condition now and compare it with that of 1932, when world prices were the lowest in four hundred years. Of course, the minister said that there is less speculation now than ever before. I disagree with that statement because I view the matter of speculation relatively. If there is less speculation it is because there is relatively less wheat, but I venture to suggest that there is a great deal of speculation with paper wheat-perhaps more relatively than ever before. The minister attacked the stabilization operations. But what would have happened1 to the west and to the entire dominion but for those operations? Moreover the stabilized price was on the basis of Fort William, not on the basis of the world price-fortunately for the western producer, for the world price, as I mentioned a few moments ago, was the lowest in four centuries.

A great deal of propaganda is coming across the ocean to western Canada to the effect that the new policy is hailed with delight in Great Britain. May I say, in passing, that I am glad to notice the better type of advertising which has lately been done in Great Britain? But I do not believe those reports present a true picture of the British attitude. For example, I have before me a copy of the leading editorial from The Miller, a British publication of February 1,	1937.
It refers to articles that have been sent from London by Mr. Grant Dexter to certain western papers, the purport of which is that there is a new feeling, a new spirit, in Great Britain towards Canadian wheat and flour since the change in the policies of the Canadian wheat board. The editorial goes on to state:
Thus, it is claimed, the campaign has demonstrated conclusively that the active resentment of the British millers and bakers during the past years to the Canadian policy of holding for a premium price has disappeared.
But it is perhaps allowable to point out at this stage that there never existed such a thing as active resentment on the part of the British millers to any Canadian policy. Canadian policy is an affair of the Canadian people, and always commands the most strict and friendly consideration of the Britisher. Milling for the British public is not an emotional pastime, but an economic service. The eompletest freedom of thought and action, to buy in the best market, and manufacture the finest product having regard to the requirements of the consumer, has been the policy of the British miller, and we maintain quite confidently that he has fulfilled his charge.
Incidentally, I am not so sure about that. Again:
The Canadian wheat policy under Mr. John McFarland had everything to commend it, had it been successful.

speechtext:
Further:
Looked at in a very practical way, its only fault was its non-success.
May I just say to hon. members opposite who laughed, that that statement comes from a British source. We were told last year that we had to win anew the confidence of the British millers. This is a quotation from a trade organ with which usually I have found myself in disagreement. But I find myself in complete agreement with the statement [DOT]that the non-success of the wheat stabilization policy was a tragedy, not to the millers but to the farmers of Canada, although it might well react ultimately upon the milling industry, because (that industry must have a source of supply, and if bankruptcy overtakes farmers over a wide area of the world the milling industry suffers accordingly. I say

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
it was a tragedy because last July, wheat was dumped in record quantities upon the market -no matter how we divide it between last year's crop and the crop of the year before or of tihe year before that. The accumulations and the 1935 crop, some 63,000,000 bushels of grain were dumped on the market and sold during July, when world stocks of wheat were the lowest in nine years and widespread drought threatened north American crops. Last night the minister said:	*
What I want to tell the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is this: If at the end of June he knew what the price of wheat was going to be, or if he knew what it was going to be at the beginning of July, or even in the middle of July, there were very few people who considered themselves authorities on the question who really thought they knew.
Does the minister, who is a member of the wheat advisory committee, recollect that on July 6-that is, in the first week in the month-the three Canadian wheat pools through their executive presented a lengthy statement, a copy of which I have in my hand, to that committee, to the government of Canada? Let me read just a portion of that statement:
We offer a few reasons why we believe the initial payment on wheat for the coming crop season should be above rather than below average production costs.
First: The restoration of buying power to agriculture is in the best interests of the entire dominion. If our main branch of agriculture is on the brink of bankruptcy every industry depending on agriculture will suffer.
Second: Largely as a result of disastrous crop conditions in exporting countries, particularly on the North American continent, the world wheat carryover is at the lowest figure in the past ten years and there has been a substantial reduction in the Canadian wheat carryover.
Third: The disastrous drought in the United States, particularly in the spring wheat belt, makes it more than probable that instead of having a substantial surplus for export, that country will again require to import a considerable quantity of Canadian wheat.
Fourth: The damage already caused to our own wheat crop by drought extending over a wide area along the southern boundary of the three prairie provinces in western Saskatchewan and eastern Alberta, and in northwestern Saskatchewan, so that the most we can look for is a fair crop, with very light crops over a great part of the west which has suffered severely in the past from partial or total crop failures.
Fifth: The setting of an initial price below production costs by the Canadian government would almost inevitably be regarded by importing countries as the price at which Canada would be prepared to dispose of its wheat, with injurious influence on world price levels.
Sixth: The bulk of the Canadian wheat crop will have been delivered and a considerable portion of it will have moved to world markets before there can be any competition from the Argentine and Australia so that the export
market price of wheat will be largely determined by the policy adopted by your committee.
Seventh: If the minimum price for wheat is set below the futures market price, the Canadian wheat board might be crippled if not destroyed, as farmers, after the experience of the present crop year would be reluctant to deliver their wheat to the board if they could secure a higher price on the open market. We believe that the continuance of the wheat board is vital to the welfare of our wheat growers under present world conditions and that any policy which would curtail the operations of the wheat board and increase the control of the private trade in marketing the Canadian crop would be against the interests of the producers.

speechtext: Does the hon. member think that there is in that statement anything that contradicts what I said last night? I would take it from the statement that what they are asking for is a set price at least no lower than the price as it was then. The price at that time was nearly the set price of last year. It does not indicate any increase.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are two things indicated in this statement. One is this-and it is the point I am making-that the Canadian wheat producers on July 6 drew the attention of the government to the fact that there was likely to be a great crop failure over the United States spring wheat belt, and over wide areas of the Canadian prairies, that stocks were the lowest in ten years, and that therefore a price above the cost of production was warranted.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The point I made last night, and which I wish to emphasize, was that in spite of that fact they did not prophesy a big increase in prices.

speechtext:
I will deal with that in a moment-the later statement of September 5. I have only forty minutes, and the minister will have an opportunity to say something at some other time.
As I said on another occasion, I left Ottawa at the end of June and motored back, and I saw this condition. When I went to my own constituency early in July, day after day I saw crops fading out until about July 10 it was well known that the whole of southern Saskatchewan would be faced with almost an entire crop failure; and yet in the face of that, day after day, the Canadian wheat board dumped wheat on the market-during that month of July nearly 63,000,000 bushels. I say that policy was inept. In the face of
The Budget-Mr. Caldwell

the condition, that existed the board should have fed the market and watched developments so that, not for our farmers only but for the entire Canadian people, we might have recouped some of the so-called losses which have been referred to so frequently in this house. And the Minister of Finance took credit for some eight million dollars in his budget statement out of the very type of price advance to which I am referring. I believe that the experts in charge of the government's marketing policy, the wheat board, ought to have so advised the government. Their policy surely constitutes something in the nature of a betrayal of trust.
But the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) says that the people approved these policies in the election of 1935, and that in the Assiniboia by-election they confirmed their approval. He also took a sly dig at the running of a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation candidate in that constituency. I wonder whether it would surprise him to know that on the day that candidate was nominated the campaign fund was $30, and that on that campaign fund we began. Out of the nickels and dimes that came in we financed the campaign. I am wondering whether the minister could say the same thing of his campaign fund. The largest contribution we received from any one person or any one source was the sum of $25. speechtext:
The farmers were forced to market their 1936 grain without the advantage of an initial price and participation certificates; that is, the wheat board method as we understand it was denied to them. I say that has meant a very serious loss to these farmers. My colleague from Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) had one of his constituents in his room the other day. After years of drought that gentleman had a good crop last year. He

Questions
raised 17,000 bushels of wheat, but owing to his obligations he had to market that grain at once. He did market it, at a price some twenty or twenty-five cents below the price he might have received if he had been able to hold it for a little while. If he had been able to market that wheat through the board and participate in the average price it is probable that he would have received a considerably greater amount of money than he did receive for his crop.
Inferences have been drawm in this house that the whole agitation of last September was inspired by someone. I do not know who that someone was. The Minister of Finance points at me and smiles.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I read some of my hon. friend's speeches on the subject.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I deny it most emphatically, and I will tell the house why I deny it. On August 28 the price was announced. The morning of the 29th I was asked for a statement, which I gave. Then that same day I got in my car and drove to Ottawa. I was ten days on the way, and during the whole of that time I neither sent nor received a communication. No one had my addresses en route. So I was not responsible for the organization of that agitation in any way whatever. On the contrary, it was the most spontaneous thing within my experience and came about to some extent from the very keen disappointment which was naturally felt on the part of the farmers. For example, on the 17th of August one of my constituents wired the Minister of Agriculture from Dins-more, Saskatchewan, as follows:
Please advise if wheat board is to function through crop year nineteen thirty-six and thirty-seven and if so what is to be the set price? Threshing is in progress and farmers are anxious to dispose of crop through wheat board if it continues to function. Wire reply.
The reply received on August 20 by that gentleman was as follows:
Wheat board will function this year. They will announce decision on nineteen thirty-six crop price shortly. I presume it would be impossible for them to make any announcement re nineteen thirty-seven crop.
Of course, the latter sentence was entirely unnecessary. The point is that apparently at that time tihe minister himself was not sure exactly what was going to happen in relation to the wheat board method of marketing.

of August the announcement was made. A moment ago the Minister of Finance pointed at me, suggesting that I had led this agitation. However, I see that it is just two minutes to six, and perhaps you will call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. To-morrow afternoon I can go on for the remainder of my time and refer to the public press records of what haippened in western Canada last autumn.
